query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with an FCC matrix, the high density of fine grain boundaries inherent to the as-built microstructure promotes accelerated oxidation (or reduction‐induced destabilization) at these boundaries during extended exposure to elevated temperatures in oxidizing or reducing atmospheres. This localized degradation weakens intergranular cohesion and leads to catastrophic failure. By reducing the grain boundary density through post‐process annealing (grain coarsening), the rate of deleterious oxide (or reduced species) formation along grain boundaries should be diminished, thereby delaying or preventing catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA exhibiting a fine, high grain boundary density FCC microstructure with potential minor compositional heterogeneity resulting from rapid solidification.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-processing annealing treatment (for example, at 950–1050 °C for selected durations) designed to coarsen the grain size without inducing undesirable phase transformations.
generation.conditions: Exposure at elevated temperatures (e.g., around 900 °C) in a controlled oxidizing atmosphere (such as air) and in a reducing gas environment (e.g., a H2-containing or CO/H2 mixture) for prolonged durations (e.g., 100 hours) to simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries and the continuity/adherence of the oxide (or altered) scale along them.
generation.mechanism: The fine grain boundaries act as fast diffusional paths for oxygen or reducing species, which leads to preferential oxidation (or destabilization) of Al and Ti at these sites. In an oxidizing environment, this results in the formation of brittle, non-adherent oxide layers (such as Al2O3 and TiO2) along grain boundaries, while in a reducing environment the protective oxide may be destabilized, exposing less resistant phases. Both cases accelerate intergranular degradation and ultimately lead to catastrophic mechanical failure. Grain coarsening reduces the total grain boundary area, thereby limiting these detrimental processes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples that undergo the annealing treatment to coarsen their grain size will exhibit slower oxidation kinetics along grain boundaries, improved continuity and adherence of the protective oxide scale, reduced crack formation, and a delay in the onset of catastrophic failure relative to as-built samples.
generation.baseline: As-built samples with a fine-grained microstructure that are expected to show rapid intergranular oxidation (or reduction-induced degradation), leading to early catastrophic failure under the specified high-temperature exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: This behavior is predicted to be relevant for exposures up to about 1000 °C in atmospheres analogous to typical oxidizing or reducing service environments. At significantly higher temperatures or under drastically different environmental conditions, other degradation mechanisms might become dominant.
generation.uncertainty: The extent to which each elemental oxidation (e.g., Al versus Ti) contributes to intergranular degradation, and the influence of any residual stresses or porosity from additive manufacturing, remain uncertain and warrant further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA: one set in the as-built condition and one set subjected to a controlled annealing treatment to induce grain coarsening. Expose both sets to 900 °C for 100 hours under both oxidizing (air) and reducing gas environments under otherwise identical conditions.
measurements: Grain size and boundary density (via SEM/EBSD)
Oxide/scale thickness, composition, and morphology at grain boundaries (via TEM/EDS)
Mechanical integrity (crack density analysis and mechanical testing such as compressive or fatigue tests)
Mass change or oxidation kinetics (via thermogravimetric analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in oxidation resistance (i.e., lower scale/spallation at grain boundaries, reduced crack formation, and improved mechanical performance) compared to the as-built samples under both oxidizing and reducing conditions, then the hypothesis that high grain boundary density governs the degradation mechanism leading to catastrophic failure is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How does an ultrafine-grain microstructure, obtained via stationary friction processing, affect the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy?. System: Equimolar AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Stationary friction processing (SFP) using a WC-cylindrical tool (12 mm diameter) at rotational speeds of 400 rpm and 1800 rpm for 5 min duration. Test conditions: Isothermal oxidation in laboratory air at 850, 950, and 1050 °C for 100 h. Findings: Grain size refined from 98 μm (as-cast) to 1 μm (SFP_400) and 0.43 μm (SFP_1800).; Phase transformation from BCC/B2 to FCC occurred, with 38% and 55% FCC fraction for SFP_400 and SFP_1800, respectively.; Surface free energy increased by 29.8% for SFP_400 and 35.2% for SFP_1800 compared to as-cast.; Oxidation kinetics decelerated by 12–20% for SFP_400 and 38–48% for SFP_1800 compared to as-cast.; Cumulative mass gain at 850 °C after 100 h was 0.33 mg/cm² (as-cast), 0.27 mg/cm² (SFP_400), and 0.17 mg/cm² (SFP_1800).; Parabolic rate constants (k_p) at 1050 °C were 23.2 × 10⁻¹³ g²·cm⁻⁴·s⁻¹ (as-cast), 18.4 × 10⁻¹³ (SFP_400), and 8.16 × 10⁻¹³ (SFP_1800).; Processed samples formed predominantly protective
